  • Okanagan (Syilx)↗Traditional regional connection in nation educational account
    Connection & source
    Traditional regional connection in nation educational account

    The Okanagan Nation Alliance educational account explicitly locates Syilx Okanagan traditional territory in south-central British Columbia and north-central Washington. These two navigation regions preserve a cross-border connection without turning modern borders into Indigenous territorial limits. Inspection: Actual geographic paragraph, line 38, source notes and publisher identification. Area measurements, archaeological conclusions and legal claims are not adopted.

    Traditional geography in Okanagan Nation Alliance educational resource. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

    Read the supporting source ↗
  • Palouse↗Named constituent people / archival regional association
    Connection & source
    Named constituent people / archival regional association

    The Archives explicitly organizes this guide by peoples living within Washington and names Palouse among the constituent peoples connected with the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation. This is an archival regional route, not a comprehensive Palouse homeland or a claim that all Palouse people belong to one government. Inspection: Actual guide methodology, lines 65–68, and Colville constituent list, lines 83–94. Underlying agency records were not reviewed.

    Historical BIA jurisdictional records organized in a Washington state finding aid. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

  • Saanich↗Traditional community / cross border regional connection
    Connection & source
    Traditional community / cross border regional connection

    The Leadership Council describes W̱SÁNEĆ/Saanich villages on the Saanich Peninsula and Southern Gulf Islands in Canada and the San Juan Islands in present Washington. Its homeland account supplies the British Columbia context. Modern bands, traditional communities and the wider people are related but not identical. These are broad historical routes, not legal-title determinations. Inspection: Actual Before the reserve system paragraph, lines 28–32; separate homeland introduction, lines 89–94. No place-name geometry, sensitive sites, oral-history retelling or territorial declaration copied.

    Pre-reserve villages described in community history published May 19, 2022. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

    Read the supporting source ↗ · Supporting source 1 ↗
  • Salish↗Named Twana community / historical regional connection
    Connection & source
    Named Twana community / historical regional connection

    The Tribe identifies Twana as a Salishan people connected with the Hood Canal drainage in western Washington. This supports Twana and a narrow route through the broader Salish access point. Salish is an overlapping language/cultural grouping here, not one government. Historical Twana communities and the present Skokomish Tribe require their own distinctions. Inspection: Actual opening historical-geographic paragraphs and public heritage-preservation account; no restricted cultural material or precise sites reproduced.

    Traditional Hood Canal connection and continuing Skokomish community, described in tribal history. Reviewed 2026-10-21.

    Read the supporting source ↗

  • Walla Walla↗Historical homeland and seasonal use connection
    Connection & source
    Historical homeland and seasonal use connection

    The CTUIR history's Life cycle and Foods section explicitly places the three constituent peoples, including Walla Walla, primarily in southeastern Washington and its neighboring cross-border region. Its lower-Columbia account separately identifies Walla Walla river communities and bands. This is a broad historical connection, not presence everywhere in the state or a merged Cayuse/Umatilla/Walla Walla identity. This supplied-study URL was independently read.
